2.text: than an ordinary run. Well-rested dogs become excited at sight of the harness,

3.text: and it is difficult to hold them in till everything is ready.

4.text: From the start, they go very fast, and want to go at a faster pace than

5.text: they can keep up afterward. Down hill their pace is quite dangerous, since

6.text: the sledge behind is liable to hit them. The sledge — long, high, and

7.text: narrow — overturns easily; and the driver, at any unevenness in the road,

8.text: has to exert the utmost care to swing the sledge, now to the right and now

9.text: to the left, and to support it by hanging down from one side or by standing

10.text: on one of the runners. Of course a light sledge, although it goes faster, is

11.text: easier to handle than a heavy one.

12.text: In short runs, dogs may be a little slower than the best reindeer or

13.text: horses; but for long distances they excel any animal used for conveyance.

14.text: I once had occasion to make, with a light sledge and good dogs, a hundred

15.text: and fifty miles in twenty-three hours, and two hundred miles in two days.

16.text: Maydell mentions that in 1869, in a race between the merchant Baramigin

17.text: and Chief Officer Anatovsky, on the Lower Kolyma, the dogs of the former

18.text: made the distance between the Anui market-place and Nishne-Kolymsk (a

19.text: hundred and fifty English miles) in fifteen hours, and the dogs of the latter

20.text: in sixteen hours. While on the Kolyma I also heard of this race; and, in my

21.text: opinion, the speed displayed on that occasion is the highest that Siberian

22.text: dogs have been known to exhibit over long distances.

23.text: In the month of March and on a good trail, a strong well-rested team

24.text: can make five hundred miles in ten days, and, after two days’ rest, will continue

25.text: with the same speed. In the winter of 1900-01 I made from four thousand

26.text: to five thousand miles with dogs, changing from time to time those that had

27.text: sore feet or were over-tired. In the spring, after a continuous drive of fourteen

28.text: days, our dogs were so tired that they would lie down on the slightest provo-

29.text: cation, and we had much trouble in rousing them from sleep after even a

30.text: moment’s stop. However, three dogs of mine were able to make the entire

31.text: journey from the mouth of the Anadyr River to the middle of Kamchatka, up

32.text: and down, and farther on to Indian Point, and still looked sleek and fat in the

33.text: summer, after two weeks’ rest. Progress with a few weak and half-starved

34.text: dogs is exceedingly slow. The opinion of Nordenskiöld, that the Chukchee dogs

35.text: show much endurance, but little speed, is evidently based on experience at a

36.text: time of famine, when the teams were weak. I saw teams that were hardly able

37.text: to drag an empty sledge, although the driver walked the whole time. The

38.text: animals had been ill fed in the fall, and well-nigh starved in the spring.

39.text: A good Anadyr team of twelve dogs can carry from four to five hundred

40.text: pounds,¹ besides a hundred pounds of their own food. Of course over a

41.text: short distance a dog-team can haul much more than that. The Kamchatka

42.text: ¹ According to the local way of measuring, two “horses” of freight. A “horse” of freight is the load

43.text: of one pack-horse, which is about 6 pud; i. e., 240 Russian pounds, or 216 pounds Avoirdupois.
